## Overview

In this module we introduce the DataFrameReader and DataFrameWriter classes and demonstrate how to read from and write to a number of data sources.


### Reading and Writing Data

* Spark can read from and write to a variety of data sources.

* The Spark SQL `DataFrameReader` and `DataFrameWriter` classes support the following data sources:
    * text
    * delimited text
    * JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
    * Apache Parquet
    * Apache ORC
    * Apache Hive
    * JDBC connection

* Spark SQL also integrates with the pandas Python package.

* Additional data sources are supported by [third-party packages](https://spark-packages.org/).

Use the csv method of the DataFrameReader class to read a delimited text file
The `csv` method is a convenience method for the following more general syntax
Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
If you use either syntax with `header` set to `True`, then Spark assumes that *every* file in the directory has a header row.

paragraphs.title: Spark does its best to infer the schema from the header row and column values
Alternatively, you can manually specify the schema
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# First, import the Spark SQL types
from pyspark.sql.types import *

# Then specify the schema as a `StructType` instance: 
schema = StructType([
    StructField("id", StringType(), True),
    StructField("birth_date", DateType(), True),
    StructField("join_date", DateType(), True),
    StructField("first_name", StringType(), True),
    StructField("last_name", StringType(), True),
    StructField("gender", StringType(), True),
    StructField("ethnicity", StringType(), True),
    StructField("student", IntegerType(), True),
    StructField("home_block", StringType(), True),
    StructField("home_lat", DoubleType(), True),
    StructField("home_lon", DoubleType(), True),
    StructField("work_lat", DoubleType(), True),
    StructField("work_lon", DoubleType(), True)
])

# Finally, pass the schema to the `DataFrameReader`:
riders2 = spark \
  .read \
  .format("csv") \
  .option("sep", ",") \
  .option("header", True) \
  .schema(schema) \
  .load("/duocar/raw/riders/")

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
We must include the header option otherwise Spark will read the header row as a valid record.

paragraphs.title: Use the text method of the `DataFrameReader` class to read an unstructured text file
Note
paragraphs.text:
%md

The default filesystem in Hadoop (and by extension CDSW) is HDFS.
The read statement above is a shortcut for
```python
weblogs = spark.read.text("hdfs:///duocar/earcloud/apache_logs/")
```
which in turn is a shortcut for
```python
weblogs = spark.read.text("hdfs:/<host:port>//duocar/earcloud/apache_logs")
```
where `<host:port>` is the host and port of the HDFS namenode.

paragraphs.title: Parse the unstructured data
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_extract

requests = weblogs.select(regexp_extract("value", "^.*\"(GET.*?)\".*$", 1).alias("request")) 

# =====================================================================================================
# Explanation of the regular expression
# =====================================================================================================
# ^
#   Indicates the start of the line or string.
#   Forces the search to begin at the very beginning of the text.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# .*
#   Any character, any number of times.
#   The combination of the dot . (any character) and the asterisk * (0 or more occurrences)
#   skips all the preceding text until the first double quotation mark is found.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# \"
#   Searches for a literal double quotation mark ("). #   The backslash \ "escapes" the double quotation mark, instructing the regular expression to look for the actual character "
#   rather than interpreting it as the start or end of a string.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (GET.*?)
#   This is capture group 1 (defined by the parentheses (...)).
#   This is the only portion that the function extracts:
#
#      GET:
#         Looks for the literal word "GET" immediately following the quotation mark.
#
#      .*?:
#         Matches any character up to the next quotation mark.
#         The question mark ? makes it "non-greedy" (or "lazy"), forcing it to stop
#         immediately at the first closing double quotation mark it encounters, rather than continuing to the end of the text.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   \"
#      Looks for the literal closing double quotation mark (") that marks the end of the request.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   .*
#      Matches any remaining text on the line after the closing quotation mark (such as HTTP status codes, byte counts, user agents, etc.).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   $
#      Indicates the end of the line or string.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

requests.head(5)

%md
## Working with object stores

Pass the appropriate prefix and path to the DataFrameReader and DataFrameWriter methods to read from and write to an object store.
For example, use the prefix `s3a` and pass the S3 bucket to read from Amazon S3

paragraphs.title: Read the demographics data from S3
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Apply the anonymous configuration directly to the SparkContext's Hadoop configuration.
sc._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set(
    "fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider",
    "org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.AnonymousAWSCredentialsProvider"
)

demographics = spark.read.csv("s3a://duocar/raw/demographics/", sep="\t", header=True, inferSchema=True)
demographics.printSchema()
demographics.show(5)

%md

If we have write permissions, then we can also write files to Amazon S3 using the `s3a` prefix.

**Important:** This code will fail when running Spark via YARN unless the worker nodes have access to the appropriate AWS credentials. 
See the documentation for your distribution of Hadoop for more details on accessing cloud storage.
